problem: Prior learning-based social navigation (RL, IRL, Navi-GAN, Social-GAN) models pedestrians individually and ignores collective group/flow behavior, so robots in dense crowds cut through groups and cause discomfort; hand-crafted cost functions do not scale to real crowds.
motivation: About 70% of pedestrians walk in social groups and humans naturally join the flow of a group with similar heading. Following such a flow should cause fewer collisions and fewer disturbances to nearby pedestrians, so the paper builds a system that recognizes groups and joins one, while a geometric local planner keeps safety.
key_idea: Extend Navi-GAN with a group pooling module (Group-Navi GAN) that associates agents to social groups and produces waypoints for the robot to follow a group's flow, layered under a geometry-based collision-avoidance local planner.
insight: Group-aware pooling helps most where groups are prevalent: it beats baselines on UNIV (73% grouped) and ZARA1 (70%) but is worse on ETH/HOTEL (18-19% grouped). Compared with goal-directed navigation without the social model, following a group reduces perceived collisions (93% to 28%) and path changes (95% to 4%) in the AMT survey. The evidence is largely qualitative and survey-based, and the ADE/FDE gains are mixed.
method: System architecture: three subsystems: state estimation (LOAM-style lidar/vision/inertial 6-DOF pose), local planning (trajectory library collision avoidance), and social navigation planning which outputs waypoints to the local planner.
Pedestrian tracking: observations contain only pedestrians, obtained by subtracting the prior map from lidar data; pedestrians are tracked and their motion patterns extracted.

Group-Navi GAN: GAN-based generative planner inspired by Navi-GAN and the extended social force model, with an intention-force generator (goal-driven) and a group-force generator (repulsion from others plus group-member interaction).

Group pooling module: an SVM (trained by Linder et al.) decides whether two agents are in the same group from speed, location and heading differences; hidden states are aggregated as h'_j = I[s_i=s_j]*cos(θi-θj)*h_j, max-pooled into an embedding, and concatenated with h_i and noise n_i for decoding.
Local collision-avoidance layer: geometry-based planner tracks the generated waypoints while avoiding obstacles at low level, ensuring safety.

setting.backbone: Group-Navi GAN (GAN with LSTM-style hidden states and group pooling, trained) + pretrained SVM group classifier + geometric local planner
setting.training_data: ETH and UCY pedestrian trajectory datasets (leave-one-out)
setting.observation: 3D lidar (Velodyne Puck) pedestrian tracks plus camera and IMU for state estimation; prior map
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints fed to a local planner (trajectory library)
setting.simulator: Custom crowd simulation (10 m x 20 m, 18 pedestrians in 6 groups) plus real world
setting.privileged: prior map used to subtract static background; assumes a known goal point for each person in datasets

numbers.eval_set_note: leave-one-out over ETH, HOTEL, UNIV, ZARA1, ZARA2; t_obs=8, t_pred=8
numbers.extra: assumes goal point per person; average over the 5 datasets
numbers.evidence: Table 1 social compliance evaluation, ADE/FDE in meters; AVG row 0.50 / 0.96

numbers.eval_set_note: 466 participants; 3 simulated scenes plus 1 real-world scene
numbers.extra: percent of participants reporting a problem (lower is better); without social model: collision 93%, path change 95%

numbers_note: No standard embodied navigation benchmark; results are trajectory-prediction errors and a user survey.
results: Group-Navi GAN outperforms Social-GAN and Navi-GAN on UNIV and ZARA1 (ADE 0.29/0.21 vs SGAN 0.36/0.21), where groups are prevalent, but has higher average error than SGAN (ADE 0.50 vs 0.39). In the AMT survey, perceived collisions dropped from 93% to 28% and forced path changes from 95% to 4% versus navigating without the social model.
limitations: Group-Navi GAN is worse than baselines on datasets with few groups (ETH, HOTEL) and needs goal points for each person.
Evaluation is small-scale (simulation with 18 people, a real-world test with 6 people) with subjective survey metrics, and no quantitative navigation metrics such as SR.
It does not model interactions between groups and scattered individuals.
builds_on: Extended social force model (Moussaid et al.)
